#### `On`

```java
public final class On
```

Exports a static method as an event handler: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `event!`. The server
has one event kind, `xdr-merge`, so there is one annotation, `XdrMerge`. The processor
generates the export that decodes the event into the method's parameters and the
`__udf_sig_<name>` export reading `event xdr-merge/1 ...`, which `event-set` checks
before binding. The parameter types are part of the kind, so a handler with another signature does not
compile. A handler returns a `Resolution`; an exception fails the call with its message.

```java
@On.XdrMerge("merge_counter")
static Resolution mergeCounter(EventRecord current, EventRecord incoming) {
    ...
    return Resolution.record(out);
}
```

A handler may also take the raw form `int name(int args, int argc)`, exported as it is with only
the signature generated; it reads the two records with `Pair.decode` and answers by returning a
resolution's `Resolution.deliver`. The name is the method's when the annotation's value is empty.

#### `On.XdrMerge`

```java
public @interface XdrMerge
```

Marks the handler of an `xdr-merge`: a method
`Resolution name(EventRecord current, EventRecord incoming)` given the record as it is on this
cluster and the one that arrived over XDR, which answers with a `Resolution`: keep-local,
take-remote, policy, delete or record. The annotation's value is the name the export gets and
`event-set` binds; the method's name when it is empty. The handler runs on an incoming XDR write
to a record this node has, live or tombstone, before the write is applied, with no clock and nothing to
write to: its answer is the only effect it has.

#### `Resolution`

```java
public final class Resolution
```

What an `xdr-merge` handler returns: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `Resolution`. Keep the
current record, apply the incoming write whole, do what the server would have done without the handler,
remove the record, or the final record.

```java
return Resolution.keepLocal();                               // drop the incoming write
return Resolution.record(pair.withNewer(out));               // these bins
```

No answer carries a TTL. The server gives the merged record the later of the two records' expirations,
and a record that never expires wins.

A resolution is checked by the server before it is taken, and one it does not accept is the handler's
failure, which the binding's `on-failure` setting decides.

#### `Resolution.keepLocal`

```java
public static Resolution keepLocal()
```

Keep the local record; the incoming write is dropped, and the source cluster is told so in a way it
counts as success.

#### `Resolution.takeRemote`

```java
public static Resolution takeRemote()
```

Apply the incoming write whole, as if it had won every bin: the incoming bins go over the current
record.

#### `Resolution.policy`

```java
public static Resolution policy()
```

Do what the server would have done without the handler. A set bound to a handler never uses bin
convergence, so this applies the incoming write, as `takeRemote` does.

#### `Resolution.delete`

```java
public static Resolution delete()
```

Remove the record on this cluster and leave a durable tombstone, so a late write cannot bring it back.
The delete is not shipped: the other cluster decides for itself, so a merge that deletes has to delete
on both sides for the two to agree. A record resolution with no bins left in it is not this: it is the
handler's failure.

#### `Resolution.expunge`

```java
public static Resolution expunge()
```

Remove the record on this cluster outright, with no tombstone, so a later write creates it again. Like
`delete`, it is not shipped to the other cluster.

#### `Resolution.record`

```java
public static Resolution record(MapBuilder bins)
```

The final record: these bins, whole - a bin not in the map, or set to nil, is deleted. The map's keys
are the bin names, so each is a string of 1 to 15 bytes. At least one bin must be left: an empty map,
or one whose values are all nil, is the handler's failure and not a deletion, which is what
`delete` is for. The builder is not used up and may still be added to before the handler
returns; it is read after the handler returns, so it must not be closed (nor made in a
try-with-resources block) in the handler.

#### `Resolution.deliver`

```java
public int deliver()
```

Sets the resolution as the result of the call and returns the status the export returns: 0, or 1 after
failing the call when the answer could not be built. The generated export of a typed handler calls it;
a handler in the raw form `int name(int args, int argc)` ends with it, as in
`return Resolution.keepLocal().deliver()`.

#### `Resolution.verdict`

```java

```

The verdict word as the server reads it: `keep-local`, `take-remote`, `policy`,
`delete`, `expunge` or `record`.

#### `EventRecord`

```java
public final class EventRecord implements RecordReader
```

One record an event hands over: each side of a merge, the current record and the incoming write. It is
read-only, and it reads like the record of a call - the same readers, through
`RecordReader` - with what an event adds: the names of its bins, the bins this side deleted,
when and by whom each bin was last written, and the few facts about the
merge that are facts about one side (`isDelete` and `isPartial` of the incoming write,
`isTombstone` of the current record). One asked of the side it is not about answers false.

A handler must be pure and convergent: both data centres merge the same two records with the sides
swapped and must land on the same record. `Pair` orders a bin's two sides by its own LUT and then
source id, which is symmetric; "mine first" is not.

A handler changes a record by answering with the bins it should have
(`Resolution.record`); `withBins` fills such an answer with every bin of this record the
handler did not decide.

```java
@On.XdrMerge("keep_higher_score")
static Resolution keepHigherScore(EventRecord current, EventRecord incoming) {
    if (incoming.isDelete()) {
        return Resolution.policy();
    }

    long mine = current.getInt("score", 0);
    long theirs = incoming.getInt("score", 0);

    return theirs > mine ? Resolution.takeRemote() : Resolution.keepLocal();
}
```

Both records are good for the whole call and for nothing after it. A handler has no record of its own
and no clock: `Udf.now` answers -1 in one, a `Udf.log` line is dropped, and the
`Record` of a record UDF is not there to read or write.

#### `EventRecord.withBins`

```java
public MapBuilder withBins(MapBuilder overrides)
```

Puts every bin of this record that `overrides` lacks into it, by position, and returns it: for a
`record` answer that changes a few bins and keeps the rest. A bin this side deleted is not put,
so in the answer it stays deleted. This prefers one side, so an `xdr-merge` handler that uses it
on the current record is not symmetric; `Pair.withNewer` is the symmetric form. It never brings
back a bin from the other side, so a bin the other side has and this one deleted stays out too. Throws
`UdfException` when a bin could not be read or put.

```java
MapBuilder out = Udf.map(4).put("visits", visits);

return Resolution.record(incoming.withBins(out));   // visits as merged, the rest as it arrived
```

#### `Pair`

```java
public final class Pair
```

The two records of a merge side by side, read bin by bin into a `Both`: the Java face of the Rust
SDK's `Pair`. `of` makes one from the two records a handler is given. A reader answers null
for a side that has no such bin or holds nil, and throws `UdfException`, with the status
`LowLevel.TYPE_MISMATCH`, for a bin of another kind.

```java
Pair pair = Pair.of(current, incoming);

Long visits = pair.getInt("visits").max();          // null when neither side has the bin
String name = pair.getString("name").newer();       // last writer wins
Long spent = pair.getInt("spent").sumInt();         // a missing side counts as 0
```

Every reader reads the bin on both sides, so each costs two reads; keep the `Both` when more than
one merge is asked of it.

#### `Pair.incomingIsNewer`

```java
public boolean incomingIsNewer(String name)
```

Whether the incoming side wrote `name` later: by the bin's time, and on a tie by the larger source
id. Both clusters compute it alike. It reads no bin, so it also answers for a bin neither side has.

#### `Pair.withNewer`

```java
public MapBuilder withNewer(MapBuilder overrides)
```

Puts into `overrides` every bin either side has that it lacks, from the side that wrote the bin
later, so a handler merges the bins it knows about and leaves the rest to the last writer of each.
Symmetric: both DCs order the two sides the same way.

A delete is a write like any other. When the side that wrote a bin later deleted it (the bin is in
that side's `EventRecord.deletedBins`), the bin is left out of the answer, which is how a
`record` answer deletes it: the older side's value is not brought back. Returns
`overrides`.

#### `Both`

```java
public final class Both<T>
```

A bin on both sides of a merge, either of which may be missing (null), with the merges a resolver
reaches for: the Java face of the Rust SDK's `Both<T>`. `Pair` builds one per bin.

```java
Both<Long> visits = pair.getInt("visits");

Long merged = visits.merge(Math::max);       // null only when neither side has the bin
Long total = visits.sumInt();                // a missing side is 0; null when both are

if (visits.current == null) {
    // the bin is new to this cluster
}
```

Every merge here answers null when both sides are missing. `current` and `incoming` are the
values themselves, to read when no merge here fits.

```java
public final T current
```

The current record's value, or null when it has no such bin or the bin is nil.

#### `Both.incoming`


The incoming write's value, or null when it has no such bin or the bin is nil.

#### `Both.incomingIsNewer`

```java
public boolean incomingIsNewer()
```

Whether the incoming side wrote this bin later: by the bin's LUT, and on a tie by source id, so
"newer" means the same on both DCs even when the clocks agreed to the millisecond.

#### `Both.newer`

```java
public T newer()
```

The side written later, by `incomingIsNewer`; whichever exists when only one does, and null when
neither does. A missing side never wins over one that exists, however late it was deleted: a merge that
must honour deletes asks `EventRecord.deleted` of the later side, as `Pair.withNewer` does.

#### `Both.older`

```java

```

The side written earlier, by `incomingIsNewer`; whichever exists when only one does, and null
when neither does.


Both sides as a list of two, the older and then the newer, either of which may be null: the order

#### `Both.currentOrIncoming`

The current value when there is one, else the incoming, else null. It prefers this cluster's side, so

#### `Both.incomingOrCurrent`


The incoming value when there is one, else the current, else null. It prefers the other cluster's side,

#### `Both.merge`

```java
public T merge(BinaryOperator<T> f)
```

Combines the two with `f` when both exist, the current value as its first argument and the
incoming as its second; the one that exists otherwise, and null when neither does. `f` is not
called with a null. For the two clusters to agree it has to give the same result with its arguments
swapped.


The larger of the two by `compareTo`; the one that exists when only one does, null when neither
does. Only for a `Comparable` T: `Long`, `Double`, `String`, `Boolean`.
Called on a `Both` of bytes, values, lists or maps it is a bad cast, not a comparison.

Value) of a `[version, value]` bin on both sides, as
`Pair.getList` reads it: the side with the higher version, ties broken by the stored bytes; null
when neither side has the bin.

```java
Value price = pair.getList("price").lwwByVersion();

if (price != null) {
    out.put("price", price);
}
```

Symmetric, idempotent and associative. For a `Both<ListValue>`.

#### `Both.maxPerKey`

```java
public static MapBuilder maxPerKey(Value current, Value incoming)
```

The per-key maximum of two maps: a new map with every key of either side, each under the larger of its
two values, or under its one value when only one side has the key. Built on the host, so it is ordered
by key and both clusters build the same bytes. Null when both sides are missing.

A side is missing when it is null, absent or nil; otherwise it must be a map whose keys are strings
or integers and whose values are integers. Anything else throws `UdfException`
(`LowLevel.TYPE_MISMATCH`), a side that is not a map included: a merge does not guess what a double
or a nested map should become. It throws with `LowLevel.REFUSED` when the host does not build the
map.

```java
MapBuilder merged = Both.maxPerKey(rec.get("seen"), theirs);
```

Symmetric (`maxPerKey(a, b)` and `maxPerKey(b, a)` are the same map), idempotent (merging
a map with itself, or with a merge it is part of, changes nothing) and associative (three sides merge to
the same map in any order): the laws a convergent merge needs. It is the merge of any map of values that
only grow; Value) is the same merge under the name of the structure it
serves.

#### `Both.sortedUnion`

```java
public static ListBuilder sortedUnion(Value current, Value incoming)
```

The union of two lists as a set: a new list with every element of either side once, sorted, so both
clusters build the same bytes whatever order the elements arrived in. Null when both sides are missing.

The elements are integers, strings or blobs: the kinds the server keys a map by, since the host
sorts them as a map built on it sorts its keys. Integers come first, by value, then strings and then
blobs, each by its bytes. An integer and a string are never the same element, however they read.

A side is missing when it is null, absent or nil; otherwise it must be a list of those kinds.
Anything else throws `UdfException` (`LowLevel.TYPE_MISMATCH`): a side that is not a list,
or an element of another kind (a double, a nested list or map, nil). It throws with
`LowLevel.REFUSED` when the host does not build the list.

Symmetric, idempotent and associative: the merge of a set that only grows. A removal needs a second
set, as the 2P-Set of the CRDT tutorial keeps one.

#### `Both.counterMerge`

```java
public static MapBuilder counterMerge(Value current, Value incoming)
```

The merge of a per-origin counter: a map of origin to count, each origin's count raised only by the
cluster it names, merged by the larger count per origin. It is Value) under
the name of the structure: the same rules, the same exceptions, and null when both sides are missing.
`counterTotal` reads the counter's value.

```java
MapBuilder counts = Both.counterMerge(current.get("hits"), incoming.get("hits"));
```

Symmetric, idempotent and associative. A count that goes down is not a count this merges: a
PN-Counter keeps a second counter for the decrements.

#### `Both.counterTotal`

```java
public static long counterTotal(Value counter)
```

The value of a per-origin counter: the sum of its counts, wrapping on overflow as `long` addition
does. 0 for a missing counter (null, absent or nil). Throws `UdfException`
(`LowLevel.TYPE_MISMATCH`) when it is not a map, or when a key is not a string or an integer or a
count is not an integer, as for Value). A built map
(`MapBuilder.asValue`) is read too, so a merged counter's total needs no second read.

```java
long total = Both.counterTotal(rec.get("hits"));
```

#### `Both.lwwByVersion`

```java
public static Value lwwByVersion(Value current, Value incoming)
```

Last writer wins by an application version: of two `[version, value]` lists, the one with the
higher version, as it is, to write back. Two equal versions are decided by the lists' stored bytes, the
greater winning, so both clusters pick the same side; two lists with the same bytes are the same either
way. Null when both sides are missing.

A side is missing when it is null, absent or nil; otherwise it must be a list of exactly two elements
whose first is an integer (anything else throws `UdfException`, `LowLevel.TYPE_MISMATCH`).
The value may be of any kind.

```java
// The write UDF moves the version and the value in one write: [version + 1, price].
Value price = Both.lwwByVersion(current.get("price"), incoming.get("price"));

if (price != null) {
    out.put("price", price);
}
```

Symmetric, idempotent and associative: it is the larger of the two by version, then by bytes, which
is a total order. The version is the application's, raised by every write that changes the value, so no
clock decides.
